clue.text: Trip had try-out of some insurance policies

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective naming such policies

indicators.note: a try that is out has been thrown out of shape, so the preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone on a trip once had a try-out of a few insurance policies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try-out' reads as one hyphenated word, but the hyphen splits it: 'try' is fodder and 'out' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Third-party cover is the basic kind of motor insurance protecting other people, so it names certain policies.

clue.text: 'Date's a herb', we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the herb is identified by its sound

blocks.note: thyme is a garden herb, pronounced like the clock word

explanation.surface: Someone insists a date is a kind of herb, apparently on hearsay.
explanation.walkthrough: Date here is not the fruit but a point on the calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: A date fixes a particular moment, so the two words are synonyms for a point in history.

clue.text: Audiotape’s gripping, A Letter From Greece

indicators.note: the word gripping says the first word holds the answer tightly inside itself

blocks.note: the four letters sit in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A recorded audio programme titled A Letter From Greece proves enthralling.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like a programme title, but only the plain sense is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth character of the Greek alphabet, so literally one of that country's letters.

clue.text: Measure of alcohol, a kind of sherry, is trifle ingredient

blocks.note: a double is a twice-sized pub measure of spirits
cream sherry is a sweet style of sherry

explanation.surface: A shot of spirits and some sherry go into the trifle, as any boozy dessert recipe insists.
explanation.walkthrough: Trifle is a British layered dessert of sponge, fruit, custard and cream, often laced with sherry.
explanation.definitionFit: Thick, high-fat cream is a standard topping layered onto that British pudding.

clue.text: ‘Reformed’ Duke – I agree, newspaper boss to cover

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it, so the words on either side enclose the duke

blocks.note: amen is said to express assent
D is the abbreviation for duke
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor agrees to cover the story of a duke who has mended his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The agreement and the editor sit on either side of the duke.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amended has been changed or corrected, which is what reformed means of a text or law.

clue.text: What might affect an athlete’s career in one of two ways?

definitions.text: What might affect an athlete’s career in one of two ways?

blocks.clueFragment: What might affect an athlete’s career
blocks.note: surface: something that shapes a sportsperson's progress over the years
setter: either the coach who guides them or the running shoe on which they literally career along

explanation.walkthrough: Career is also a verb, to rush along, so the shoe affects how an athlete careers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a coach who develops sportspeople and a sports shoe worn for running.

clue.text: Primarily, amicable mademoiselle I'll esteem?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each following word counts

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A Frenchman wonders whether a friendly young woman is the one he will cherish above all.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a friendly French girl one holds dear.
explanation.definitionFit: French for a female friend or girlfriend, a phrase English borrows as in mon amie.

clue.text: Witches and I end up touring Pacific lands

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top
touring means going round, so one piece travels around the others

blocks.note: crones are old hags, the stock witches of folklore
taken as written
an end is a goal or aim

explanation.surface: A witch's coven sets off on a voyage around the islands of the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed aim splits after its second letter to hold the witches and the I.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a region of thousands of small islands in the western Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Receiving pursuit, shake a rein of a horse

indicators.note: shaking jumbles things up, so the letters that follow are rearranged
receiving means taking something in, so the jumbled letters hold another word

blocks.note: the fodder letters
a quest is a search or pursuit

explanation.surface: A rider in a chase gives the reins a shake to urge the mount on.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to horse riding and horsemanship.

clue.text: Everyman – so healthy! – knocked back enormous quantity of booze

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the word for healthy runs in reverse

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so the setter's name stands for me
thus means so, in that way
hale means strong and healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of good health despite downing a vast amount of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Knocked back looks like drinking, matching the booze, but it reverses the word for healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine bottle eight times standard size, named after the biblical patriarch who lived longest.

clue.text: Fawn in pie crust

indicators.note: in says the letters are lodged inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A young deer has been baked into a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: Fawn looks like the baby deer; here it is the pale brown colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a pale greyish-yellow or beige shade, like unbleached linen.

clue.text: Romantic tale is long, sordid novel

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the preceding letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a love story as overlong and seedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel looks like the book being reviewed, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1998 romantic film with Gwyneth Paltrow, whose plot splits on catching or missing a train.

clue.text: Wren has designs for this political assembly

blocks.note: surface: the architect Christopher Wren drawing plans for a building
setter: a small songbird has designs on, meaning wants to eat, its usual food

explanation.walkthrough: Wren suggests the architect of St Paul's, but it is the bird, and its feeding gives a pun on a historic assembly.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1521 imperial council held in a German city that condemned Martin Luther; diet means a formal assembly.

clue.text: Turns before dock that’s damper

blocks.note: food that turns goes off, or spoils
a port is where ships dock

explanation.surface: A ship turns about before coming in to berth, which feels a bit flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Damper reads as something wet, but it means a person who dampens enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who ruins others' fun is a killjoy who puts a damper on proceedings.

clue.text: A heartless romance leads to bother for lover

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is removed from the word for romance

blocks.note: taken as written
romance is a genre of fiction
ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A callous affair causes trouble for the person in love.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter, the T.
explanation.definitionFit: An enthusiast or devotee of some pursuit is a fan, so a lover of opera or jazz.

clue.text: Dour rival displayed impatience for Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two sounds trade places

blocks.note: a foe is a rival, and someone impatient paced up and down; swapping the opening F and P sounds of the pair gives the spelling here

explanation.surface: A grim opponent showed he was fed up waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the F and P sounds of the two words; the first word is spelt as the informal pot or chamber-pot prefix.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a stern, humourless, disapproving expression is what a solemn, unsmiling look conveys.

clue.text: Perhaps Bambi seen in rejigged order, Ena's introduction included twice

indicators.note: rejigged means rearranged, so the following word changes its order
an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter of Ena is used
included means put inside, so letters are slotted into the rearranged word

blocks.note: the fodder letters
the initial of the name
the same initial a second time

explanation.surface: Bambi turns up in a reshuffled line-up that features Ena twice.
explanation.walkthrough: Bambi is the Disney fawn; Perhaps marks him as one example of the species.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi was a roe deer in Felix Salten's original book, so an example of that small European species.

clue.text: Controlled creep, by 'eck

blocks.note: to inch is to creep forward slowly
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in the north of England exclaims at a creep being kept in line.
explanation.walkthrough: By 'eck is a northern English exclamation of surprise; here by just places one piece beside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Held in check is an idiom for restrained or kept under control.

clue.text: Skirt (it’s chiné) as regularly worn by divinity

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A deity wears a skirt of chiné, a fabric with a mottled woven pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: A major Hindu god, the eighth avatar of Vishnu, so a divine being.

clue.text: ‘Abaci to Xeroxes’: retrospective includes unusual items

indicators.note: includes says the letters are contained within the quoted words
retrospective means looking backwards, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A museum retrospective of office machines, from abacuses to photocopiers, features some curiosities.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means curious or strange objects from far away, a plural of exotic things.

clue.text: To some extent commend, or second?

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so just a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone at a meeting asks whether to praise a motion or merely back it.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to give it formal support, which is to back or approve it.

clue.text: What might rattle 'mid worst snow?

indicators.note: to rattle is to shake about, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Something shakes noisily in the middle of a blizzard.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: these panes do rattle in bad weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra outer panes fitted to protect a house in bad weather, liable to shake in a blizzard.

clue.text: Join up with part of orchestra

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to abut is to adjoin or join at an edge

explanation.surface: A musician is invited to sign up with a section of the orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: Join up looks like a phrasal verb meaning enlist, but up is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The large low-pitched brass instrument is one member of the orchestra's brass section.

clue.text: Look — with eyes half-closed, a parliamentarian

blocks.note: first meaning: to squint or gaze narrowly
second meaning: a member of the House of Lords

explanation.walkthrough: Eyes half-closed looks like it could be removing half of a word, but it describes the way of looking.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to gaze with difficulty, and the noun a noble who sits in Britain's upper house.

clue.text: Mother getting in on Sultan's territory

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother gains entry to a ruler's land.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulf state on the Arabian peninsula is ruled by a sultan, so it is his domain.

clue.text: Green with plan to recycle

blocks.note: a chart is a map or plan
to recycle something is to use it again

explanation.surface: An environmentalist has a scheme for recycling.
explanation.walkthrough: Green looks like environmental, matching recycle, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A vivid yellowish-green colour, named after a French liqueur of that hue.

clue.text: God, person with lisp’s angry

indicators.note: a lisper says th for s, so the word is heard as such a speaker pronounces it

blocks.note: sore means angry, and with a lisp the opening s becomes th

explanation.surface: A deity complains, in a lisping voice, that he is cross.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse god of thunder who wields a hammer, a deity of Scandinavian myth.

clue.text: Fibre provided by pathetic meals — 'moderate sandwiches'

indicators.note: something pathetic is a poor mess, so the following letters are jumbled
sandwiching means holding between two layers, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: to chair a meeting is to moderate it
the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Sad meals of modest sandwiches are said to provide roughage.
explanation.walkthrough: Fibre suggests diet next to the meals, but it is a textile.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft hair from the animal is spun into a fine woollen textile used for coats.
